analysis.one_liner: Strengthens workers' rights to form unions, strike, and sue over retaliation, and raises penalties on employers who break labor law.
analysis.headline: The Senate Labor Committee reported the bill favorably and placed it on the Senate calendar, but it never received a floor vote before Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would rewrite federal labor law to make it much easier for workers to form unions and bargain collectively. It would widen who counts as an "employee" (including many gig workers), let unions win elections even when an employer broke the rules, ban employers from forcing workers into anti-union meetings, make it an unfair labor practice to permanently replace strikers, allow sympathetic "secondary" strikes at other companies, force binding arbitration to settle a first contract, and raise fines on companies that violate labor law from a few hundred dollars to as much as $50,000 per violation, with personal liability for executives. The Senate Labor Committee approved it, but the bill sat on the Senate calendar and never came to a vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers who want to organize would gain the most: faster and fairer union elections, protection from being permanently replaced for striking, an end to mandatory anti-union meetings, the right to join class-action lawsuits over workplace abuses instead of being forced into individual arbitration, and real financial penalties against employers who retaliate. Gig and contract workers would gain employee status if they meet the bill's test. Unions would gain members, revenue through fair-share fees in all states, and a binding arbitration process for first contracts.

how_it_helps.text: Closes the 'independent contractor' and supervisor loopholes so more workers — including many gig workers — count as employees with organizing rights, and broadens the joint-employer rule so companies that actually control workers' conditions can be held responsible.

Makes it an unfair labor practice to permanently replace strikers, to discriminate against strikers, or to force workers into anti-union meetings, and removes the ban on sympathetic (secondary) strikes.

Bars employers from making workers sign away their right to join class or collective lawsuits, voiding forced arbitration agreements that currently channel many workplace disputes into private, individual arbitration.

Adds real teeth: civil penalties up to $50,000 per violation (double for repeat offenders), personal liability for directors and officers, back and front pay plus double liquidated damages for fired workers, and court enforcement of labor board orders that currently can sit unenforced.

Speeds up union elections and, if the employer illegally interferes and a majority of workers had signed union cards, certifies the union without a rerun election; it also requires binding arbitration to settle a first contract if mediation fails after 120 days, and lets unions win elections by mail, electronically, or off employer property.

analysis.who_pays: Employers — especially large companies that resist unionization — would pay the cost: civil fines up to $50,000 per violation, doubled damages for firing or economically harming strikers, personal liability for officers, mandatory first-contract arbitration, and lost ability to require workers to sign away class-action rights. Some consumers could see higher prices if labor costs rise.

drawbacks.text: Mandatory-interest arbitration for first contracts removes some bargaining outcomes from the two parties at the table and hands them to a three-person arbitration panel, whose binding decision may not match what either side would have negotiated.
Reclassifying contractors as employees could change or end the independent status of some gig-economy and freelance workers, a cost an honest supporter of the bill would acknowledge.

Permitting secondary strikes allows work stoppages to spread to companies that are not the direct employer in the dispute, and fair-share fees can be required even in states whose voters had barred them.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits to workers are broad and concrete: real penalties, faster elections, first-contract arbitration, and restored access to collective legal action. The costs and objections are real: binding arbitration on first contracts overrides the negotiated agreement of both parties to that contract; classified as employees, some gig workers might lose the flexibility of independent work; secondary strikes can spread business disruptions beyond the disputing employer; and requiring fee contributions in all 50 states overrides state right-to-work choices. On the other side, the bill's critics — mainly employers and business groups — say it exposes companies to large damage awards and dilutes employee choice by letting unions certify representation without a lost election.

outcome.mechanism: The Senate Labor Committee approved it and put it on the Senate calendar, but no floor vote ever happened and the Congress ended.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced in February 2023 and referred to the Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee.
On June 21, 2023, the committee ordered the bill reported favorably without amendment, and Senator Sanders reported it to the Senate on July 18, 2023.

The bill was placed on the Senate Legislative Calendar under General Orders (Calendar No. 133) — the waiting list for floor consideration — and was never taken up before the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025.

It had 48 Senate cosponsors, all Democrats plus one Independent, and no Republican support; with 49 Senate Republicans, the bill had no realistic path to the 60 votes normally needed to break a filibuster and reach a final vote.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers, who keep the current rules under which union organizing remains difficult and violations carry penalties of a few hundred dollars to a few thousand.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Employers, who keep the current rules

for.name: Bernie Sanders
for.role: U.S. Senator (sponsor), Chairman of the Senate HELP Committee
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and, as committee chair, reported it favorably out of the HELP Committee and placed it on the Senate calendar.

for.name: 47 of 48 Senate Democrats and 1 of 4 Independents
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, including Chuck Schumer and nearly the entire Democratic caucus.

for.name: Organized labor
for.what_they_did: Backed the PRO Act as labor's top legislative priority; the bill is named for former AFL-CIO president Richard Trumka.

against.name: Business and employer lobbies
against.role: Major employer associations and business groups
against.what_they_did: Opposed the bill publicly in prior years and again in this Congress, arguing it would raise labor costs and expand union power; their opposition underpinned unified Republican resistance.

against.name: 49 of 49 Senate Republicans
against.what_they_did: None cosponsored the bill, providing the unified opposition bloc that made the bill unable to reach the 60 votes needed to advance on the Senate floor.

sides.party_line_note: Support was almost entirely Democratic: 47 of 48 Senate Democrats plus one Independent (King) cosponsored, and no Republican did. The bill died in a Senate where 49 Republicans were enough to block any vote it could not get 60 votes to reach.

industries.industry: Employers (large and small), especially in low-wage and anti-union sectors like retail, logistics, and food service
industries.note: The bill removes the most effective tools for keeping unions out — captive meetings, permanent striker replacement, forced arbitration clauses, and drawn-out elections — and adds fines up to $50,000 per violation plus personal officer liability. Its interest runs against the workers the bill protects.

The ABC-style employee test would reclassify many app-based and contract workers as employees, entitling them to organize and to minimum protections, which would raise platform labor costs. That cost is the price of extending basic labor rights to these workers.

Unions gain easier elections, secondary strikes, fair-share fees overriding state right-to-work laws, and binding first-contract arbitration, which would grow membership and revenue. Here the industry's interest and workers' organizing rights run together, though critics note unions are also the bill's direct beneficiaries.
